newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-SACCHI TRIES TO NEGOTIATE PEACE AT MILAN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-SACCHI TRIES TO NEGOTIATE PEACE AT MILAN.

text.p: Arrigo Sacchi has no experience in political diplomacy but his peace-making efforts at troubled Milan have even won praise from former US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger.
"In Italy, the only true strategist I know is Arrigo Sacchi," said Kissinger on a recent visit to San Siro, "he's a Machaevellian genius."

Ex-national coach Sacchi will unveil his latest scheme in crisis-management on Sunday, deploying the same Milan side that won the league title last year for a vital clash with second-placed Sampdoria.
With talk of a player purge at the end of the season, Sacchi's manoeuvre should keep the peace among his team's old guard.
"We must stay calm," Sacchi said this week, "we cannot throw away 10 years of history."

Against Sampdoria, there are recalls for Montenegrin Dejan Savicevic and Liberian George Weah, out since Christmas with an ankle injury, and defender Alessandro Costacurta, suspended for last week's disastrous 3-1 defeat at Verona.
In defence, Dutch international Michael Reiziger, a disappointment since his transfer from Ajax last summer, makes way for 19-year-old Francesco Coco.
But with Milan out of Europe after home defeat to Norwegian club Rosenborg and 10th in the table after seven league defeats, Sacchi's fragile peace is starting to look like the calm before the storm.
"Ten years at the summit of soccer, its stresses and pressures, are finally taking their toll," admitted Vincenzo Pincolini, Milan's fitness specialist.
In a recent meeting with dissatisfied fans, deputy club president Adriano Galliani promised to rebuild the team.

"We're working to build a grand, new Milan," Galliani told Gazzetta dello Sport on Tuesday, "last year Real Madrid failed in Europe but still bought in some tremendous players. Why shouldn't we do the same?"
Respected sports magazine Guerin Sportivo this week published a possible line-up for the 1997/98 season that included just three members of the great Milan sides of the recent past.

New faces included Patrick Kluivert and Winston Bogarde from Ajax, Bayern Munich defender Christian Ziege, Alessandro Nesta from Lazio and Fabrizio Ravanelli, currently with Middlesbrough in England's premier league.
There is widespread speculation that Dejan Savicevic, Zvonimir Boban, Costacurta and Sebastiano Rossi will leave the club at the end of the season.
But critics suggest Milan no longer have the cash to buy themselves out of trouble -- the club ended last year with debts amounting to 44 billion lire ($27.3 million), the worst in serie A.

Others say the current malaise stems not just from the players but the club itself, wondering aloud about the wisdom of refusing to renew Fabio Capello's contract after he had won his fourth title in five years last summer. Capello left to become coach of Real Madrid and has guided them to the top of the Spanish league.
The club's former striker Gianni Rivera blames no lesser a figure than Milan president and former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi.

"Capello was becoming too famous," Rivera told news weekly "L'Espresso" this week, "Berlusconi wanted to use football to demonstrate his ability to come first in everything. But Capello was putting him in the shadow."
By trying to right their error and go back to the future with another former manager in Sacchi, Berlusconi might have made a second mistake.

Many of Milan's first-team players had already fallen out with Sacchi when he managed the national side. A dressing room bust-up with Roberto Baggio, whom he had dropped for Italy, confirmed fans worst fears.
Baggio's presence in the team for Sunday's clash with Sampdoria confirms that Sacchi's "Machaevellian" skills have brought peace to one battle.
But the war over Milan's future is only just beginning.
